passages.title: The lotus pond in Paradise
passages.text: ある日の事でございます。御釈迦様は極楽の蓮池のふちを、独りでぶらぶら御歩きになっていらっしゃいました。池の中に咲いている蓮の花は、みんな玉のようにまっ白で、そのまん中にある金色の蕊からは、何とも云えない好い匂が、絶間なくあたりへ溢れて居ります。極楽は丁度朝なのでございましょう。
passages.reference: It happened one day. The Buddha was strolling alone along the edge of the lotus pond in Paradise. The lotus flowers blooming in the pond were all as white as pearls, and from the golden stamens at their centers an indescribably sweet fragrance flowed out ceaselessly into the air around them. It must have been morning in Paradise.
passages.register: unhurried storyteller's narration in English, gently reverent toward the Buddha (echoing the source's ございます and honorific 御〜になる)
keyPoints: 御釈迦様 = the Buddha; the honorific 御〜になる forms become a reverent tone, not literal honorific words
極楽 = Paradise (the Buddhist Pure Land)
玉のようにまっ白 = as white as pearls/jewels
絶間なく…溢れて居ります = flows out ceaselessly
〜なのでございましょう = narrator's conjecture: 'It must have been morning'
passages.notes: The narrator's ございます style is a storyteller's polite voice addressed to listeners; carry it with a measured, slightly formal English rhythm rather than archaisms. The final sentence is a guess by the narrator, so keep the modal ('must have been').

passages.title: But I am dying
passages.text: 自分は透き徹るほど深く見えるこの黒眼の色沢を眺めて、これでも死ぬのかと思った。それで、ねんごろに枕の傍へ口を付けて、死ぬんじゃなかろうね、大丈夫だろうね、とまた聞き返した。すると女は黒い眼を眠そうに睜たまま、やっぱり静かな声で、でも、死ぬんですもの、仕方がないわと云った。
passages.reference: I gazed at the sheen of those black eyes, which looked deep enough to see right through, and thought: can she really be dying? So I leaned close to her pillow and asked again, tenderly, "You're not going to die, are you? You'll be all right, won't you?" The woman kept her black eyes open, drowsily, and said in the same quiet voice, "But I am dying. There's nothing to be done."
passages.register: literary first-person narrative English, restrained and dreamlike; dialogue can be set off with quotation marks
keyPoints: 自分 = the narrator 'I' (not 'myself')
透き徹るほど深く見える = so deep one could see right through them
ねんごろに = tenderly, solicitously
眠そうに睜たまま = keeping her eyes open, drowsily
死ぬんですもの、仕方がないわ = plaintive feminine justification: 'But I am dying. It can't be helped.'
passages.notes: Soseki embeds speech without quotation marks (と云った, と聞き返した); English readers expect quotation marks, which is acceptable. もの adds a soft, almost childlike 'but...' of justification, and わ marks the woman's gentle feminine speech; render the tone rather than the particles.

passages.title: Waiting for the whistle
passages.text: 或曇った冬の日暮である。私は横須賀発上り二等客車の隅に腰を下して、ぼんやり発車の笛を待っていた。とうに電燈のついた客車の中には、珍らしく私の外に一人も乗客はいなかった。外を覗くと、うす暗いプラットフォオムにも、今日は珍しく見送りの人影さえ跡を絶って、唯、檻に入れられた小犬が一匹、時々悲しそうに、吠え立てていた。これらはその時の私の心もちと、不思議な位似つかわしい景色だった。私の頭の中には云いようのない疲労と倦怠とが、まるで雪曇りの空のようなどんよりした影を落していた。私は外套のポッケットへじっと両手をつっこんだまま、そこにはいっている夕刊を出して見ようと云う元気さえ起らなかった。
passages.reference: It was dusk on an overcast winter day. I was sitting in a corner of a second-class carriage on the up train from Yokosuka, idly waiting for the departure whistle. The lights in the carriage had long since been switched on, and for once there was not a single passenger besides me. When I looked out, even the dim platform was unusually deserted today, without so much as anyone seeing a traveler off; there was only a puppy shut in a cage, barking mournfully now and then. All this matched my mood at that moment to an uncanny degree. An indescribable weariness and ennui hung over my mind like the heavy shadow of a sky clouded over before snow. With both hands thrust deep into the pockets of my overcoat, I could not even summon the energy to take out the evening paper that was in one of them.
passages.register: literary first-person past-tense narrative English, somber and precise
keyPoints: 上り = the up train (bound toward Tokyo)
二等客車 = second-class carriage
見送りの人影さえ跡を絶って = not even anyone seeing travelers off
云いようのない疲労と倦怠 = indescribable weariness and ennui; 雪曇りの空 = sky clouded over before snow
元気さえ起らなかった = could not even summon the energy
passages.notes: The opening noun-sentence (或曇った冬の日暮である) sets the scene; 'It was dusk on an overcast winter day' keeps its abruptness. 不思議な位似つかわしい is 'matched ... to an uncanny degree', not 'strangely suitable'. Keep the long final sentence as one weary movement.

passages.title: Friend or foe at the border
passages.text: 初め、たがいに顔を知り合わない間は、二人は敵か味方かというような感じがして、ろくろくものもいいませんでしたけれど、いつしか二人は仲よしになってしまいました。二人は、ほかに話をする相手もなく退屈であったからであります。そして、春の日は長く、うららかに、頭の上に照り輝いているからでありました。
passages.reference: At first, before they knew each other, each of the two felt unsure whether the other was friend or foe, and they barely spoke a word. But before long they had become good friends. They had no one else to talk to and were bored, and besides, the spring days were long, and the sun shone mild and bright above their heads.
passages.register: gentle storybook narration in plain past-tense English
keyPoints: 敵か味方か = friend or foe
ろくろくものもいいませんでした = hardly said a word
いつしか = before long / before they knew it
〜からであります / 〜からでありました = two reasons, the second added with そして ('and besides')
うららかに照り輝いている = the sun shone mild and bright (spring warmth)
passages.notes: The であります narration is an old-fashioned children's-story politeness; plain storybook English carries it. The reasons come after the result in Japanese (…からであります); English can keep that order with 'They had ... and besides ...'.

passages.title: Two sweet buns every morning
passages.text:
駅の近くの小さなパン屋で美咲が働き始めて、三か月がたった。毎朝七時になると、同じおじいさんが店に来る。いつも買うのは、あんパンを二つだけだ。
美咲は、「一人で二つも食べるんですか」と聞いてみたかったが、なかなか聞くことができなかった。おじいさんはいつも静かにお金を払って、「ありがとう」と小さな声で言って帰っていく。
ある雨の朝、おじいさんは来なかった。次の日も、その次の日も来なかった。美咲が心配になって店長に話すと、店長は「具合が悪いんじゃないかな」と言った。
passages.reference:
Misaki had been working at the little bakery near the station for three months. Every morning at seven, the same old man came into the shop. He always bought just two anpan, sweet bean buns.
Misaki wanted to ask him, "Do you eat two all by yourself?", but she could never quite bring herself to. The old man always paid quietly, said "Thank you" in a small voice, and left.
One rainy morning, the old man didn't come. He didn't come the next day, or the day after that. When Misaki, growing worried, mentioned it to the manager, he said, "Maybe he's not feeling well."
passages.register: plain past-tense narrative English, simple and warm
keyPoints: Japanese mixes past and present tense (たった / 来る / 帰っていく); English narration should stay consistently in the past
二つも = two whole buns (surprise at the number)
聞いてみたかったが、なかなか聞くことができなかった = wanted to ask but could never quite bring herself to
店長 = the (shop) manager
具合が悪いんじゃないかな = hedged guess: 'Maybe he's not feeling well'
passages.notes: The present-tense habitual sentences (来る, いつも買うのは…だ) describe routine inside a past narrative; English uses the simple past. あんパン can be kept as 'anpan' with a gloss or rendered 'sweet bean buns'.

passages.title: Hydrangeas in the rainy season
passages.text: 六月に入ると、町は急に静かになる。毎日のように細かい雨が降り、部屋の中に干した洗濯物はなかなか乾かない。それでも私は、この季節が嫌いではない。家の前の小さな庭では、あじさいが少しずつ色を変えていく。最初は薄い緑だった花が、雨のたびに青くなり、月の終わりには紫に近くなる。朝、傘をさして家を出る前に、その日の花の色を確かめるのが、私の小さな楽しみになっている。
passages.reference: Once June arrives, the town suddenly goes quiet. A fine rain falls almost every day, and laundry hung up indoors takes forever to dry. Even so, I don't dislike this season. In the little garden in front of my house, the hydrangeas change color bit by bit. Blossoms that start out pale green turn bluer with each rain, and by the end of the month they are nearly purple. Checking the color of the flowers each morning before I head out under my umbrella has become one of my small pleasures.
passages.register: reflective first-person essay English, present tense
keyPoints: 嫌いではない = litotes: 'I don't dislike' (not 'I like')
毎日のように = almost every day
なかなか乾かない = takes forever / won't dry
雨のたびに = with each rain
〜のが楽しみになっている = has become a (small) pleasure
passages.notes: The essay is in habitual present; keep English in the present. 嫌いではない is deliberately understated and should stay understated.

passages.title: My father's old bicycle
passages.text: 実家を片づけていたら、物置の奥から古い自転車が出てきた。父が若いころ通勤に使っていたもので、ハンドルにはさびが浮き、タイヤはすっかり空気が抜けていた。捨てるつもりで外に運び出したものの、どうしても手放す気になれなかった。子どものころ、この自転車の荷台に乗せてもらって、川沿いの道を何度も走ったことを思い出したからだ。結局、自転車屋に持ち込んで直してもらうことにした。修理代は新しいものを買うのとほとんど変わらなかったが、不思議と惜しいとは思わなかった。
passages.reference: While I was clearing out my parents' house, an old bicycle turned up at the back of the shed. It was the one my father had ridden to work when he was young; the handlebars were spotted with rust and the tires were completely flat. I carried it outside meaning to throw it away, but I just couldn't bring myself to part with it. I had remembered how, as a child, I used to ride on its rear rack while my father pedaled along the riverside path, over and over. In the end I decided to take it to a bike shop and have it fixed. The repair cost almost as much as a new bike, but strangely, I didn't feel it was money wasted.
passages.register: personal essay English, first person past tense, understated
keyPoints: 実家 = parents' (family) home, not 'my house'
〜ものの = although / but
手放す気になれなかった = couldn't bring myself to part with it
荷台に乗せてもらって = implied subject: father gave the child rides on the rear rack
惜しいとは思わなかった = didn't feel it was a waste (of money)
passages.notes: 乗せてもらって hides who was pedaling; a good translation makes the father's role explicit. The reason clause (…思い出したからだ) explains the previous sentence and can be rendered as a separate sentence in the pluperfect.

passages.title: The bookshop on the corner
passages.text: There is a small bookshop on the corner near my apartment. It is so narrow that two people cannot pass each other between the shelves. The owner, an old woman, is always reading behind the counter, and she rarely looks up when customers come in. At first I thought she was unfriendly. But one day, when I was looking for a book about birds, she stood up without a word and handed me exactly the one I wanted. Since then, I have stopped by almost every week.
passages.reference: アパートの近くの角に、小さな本屋がある。とても狭くて、本棚の間では二人がすれ違うこともできない。店主のおばあさんはいつもカウンターの奥で本を読んでいて、客が入ってきてもほとんど顔を上げない。最初は、無愛想な人だと思っていた。ところがある日、私が鳥の本を探していると、おばあさんは何も言わずに立ち上がり、私がまさに欲しかった一冊を差し出してくれた。それ以来、私はほとんど毎週その店に寄っている。
passages.register: plain written Japanese narrative (だ/である調, 普通体), first person
keyPoints: so narrow that ... cannot = 狭くて…できない / 〜ほど狭い
rarely looks up = ほとんど顔を上げない
unfriendly = 無愛想
handed me = 差し出してくれた (くれる for a favor to the narrator)
Since then, have stopped by = それ以来…寄っている (ongoing habit, ている)
passages.notes: Drop the redundant 'my' where Japanese would omit it (アパートの近く). Use てくれた to show the owner's act as a kindness to the narrator; the present perfect habit becomes ている.

passages.title: Airing the winter quilt
passages.text: Every year, when the first cold wind blows in late October, my grandmother takes out her winter quilt and hangs it in the sun. She says that a quilt dried in autumn sunlight smells like the harvest. As a child, I laughed at her, but now that I live alone in the city, I find myself doing the same thing on my narrow balcony. The smell is not quite the same, of course. Still, when I bury my face in the warm cloth at night, I feel, for a moment, that I am back in her house.
passages.reference: 毎年、十月の終わりに最初の冷たい風が吹くと、祖母は冬用の布団を出して日に干す。秋の日差しで干した布団は収穫の匂いがするのだと、祖母は言う。子どものころはそれを笑っていたが、都会で一人暮らしをしている今、気がつけば私も狭いベランダで同じことをしている。もちろん、匂いがまったく同じというわけではない。それでも夜、温かい布団に顔をうずめると、ほんの一瞬、祖母の家に戻ったような気がするのだ。
passages.register: reflective written Japanese essay, plain style (だ/である調) with のだ for explanation
keyPoints: quilt = 布団 (the Japanese futon quilt), hangs it in the sun = 日に干す
I find myself doing = 気がつけば…している
not quite the same = まったく同じというわけではない (partial negation)
I feel that I am back = 戻ったような気がする
my grandmother as family member = 祖母 (not おばあさん in written narrative)
passages.notes: Use 祖母 for one's own grandmother in written prose. 'Not quite the same' is a partial negation (というわけではない), not 全然違う. A closing のだ gives the essay its reflective, explanatory cadence.

passages.title: The 6:42
passages.text: The station had been closed for eleven years, yet the timetable was still pinned to the wall of the waiting room, its paper yellowed and curling at the edges. Kenji ran his finger down the column of departures until he found the 6:42, the train he had taken every morning of his high-school life. He had half expected to feel something - grief, perhaps, or relief. Instead he felt only a vague embarrassment, as though he had walked into a stranger's house and found his own coat hanging by the door.
passages.reference: 駅が廃止されてから十一年がたつというのに、待合室の壁にはまだ時刻表が貼られたままになっていた。紙は黄ばみ、端が丸まっている。健二は発車時刻の列を指でたどり、六時四十二分のところで止めた。高校時代、毎朝欠かさず乗っていた列車だ。何かしら込み上げてくるものがあるだろうと、半ば予期していた。悲しみか、あるいは安堵か。だが実際に感じたのは、漠然とした気恥ずかしさだけだった。まるで見知らぬ人の家に上がり込んだら、戸口に自分のコートが掛かっていた、とでもいうような。
passages.register: literary written Japanese, plain past narrative (た形) with free indirect nuance
keyPoints: yet = というのに (concessive surprise)
still pinned = 貼られたままになっていた (〜たまま for an unchanged state)
had half expected to feel something = 何かしら込み上げてくるものがあるだろうと半ば予期していた
vague embarrassment = 漠然とした気恥ずかしさ
as though ... = まるで…とでもいうような (simile left as a fragment)
passages.notes: Japanese literary prose readily splits the long English sentences and can end on a fragment (悲しみか、あるいは安堵か。/ …とでもいうような。). Keep 6:42 as 六時四十二分 and render 'every morning of his high-school life' as 高校時代、毎朝.

passages.title: Ramen on Saturday
passages.text:
A：ねえ、土曜日ひま？
B：うん、特に予定ないけど。どうして？
A：駅前に新しいラーメン屋ができたんだって。一緒に行かない？
B：いいね！何時ごろにする？
A：昼は混むから、十一時に駅で待ち合わせしよう。
B：わかった。じゃ、遅れないでね。
A：それはこっちのセリフだよ。
passages.reference:
A: Hey, you free Saturday?
B: Yeah, nothing planned. Why?
A: I heard a new ramen place opened in front of the station. Wanna go?
B: Sounds good! What time?
A: It gets packed at lunch, so let's meet at the station at eleven.
B: Okay. Don't be late, then.
A: Look who's talking.
passages.register: casual spoken English between close friends (contractions, dropped words)
keyPoints: casual register throughout: 'you free', 'Wanna go?', not 'Are you available?'
〜んだって = hearsay: 'I heard' / 'apparently'
行かない？ = an invitation, not a negative question
昼は混むから = it gets crowded/packed at lunch
それはこっちのセリフだよ = idiom: 'Look who's talking' / 'I should be saying that'
passages.notes: The Japanese drops particles and uses plain forms; a stiff English rendering ('Do you have free time on Saturday?') misses the register. こっちのセリフ must not be translated literally as 'that's my line'.

passages.title: Sold out in white
passages.text:
A：いらっしゃいませ。何かお探しですか。
B：あの、このシャツの白はありますか。
A：申し訳ございません。白は今、売り切れておりまして…。黒でしたらございますが。
B：そうですか。黒はちょっと…。いつ入りますか。
A：来週の水曜日に入荷する予定でございます。
B：じゃあ、また来週来ます。
A：かしこまりました。お待ちしております。
passages.reference:
A: Hello! Are you looking for anything in particular?
B: Um, do you have this shirt in white?
A: I'm very sorry, white is sold out at the moment... We do have it in black, though.
B: I see. Black's not really... When will you get more in?
A: We're expecting a delivery next Wednesday.
B: Okay, I'll come back next week, then.
A: Certainly. We'll look forward to seeing you.
passages.register: polite customer-service English from the clerk; plain polite English from the customer
keyPoints: いらっしゃいませ = a greeting ('Hello!' / 'Hi there'), not 'Welcome'
売り切れておりまして… = trailing apologetic explanation: 'is sold out at the moment...'
黒はちょっと… = implied refusal: 'Black's not really...' (keep it unfinished)
入荷する予定 = expecting a delivery / new stock
お待ちしております = 'We'll look forward to seeing you'
passages.notes: The clerk's humble forms (ございます, おります) map to service politeness in English (Certainly, We do have...), not to archaic phrasing. The customer's ちょっと… is a soft refusal and should stay soft.

passages.title: Calling the clinic
passages.text:
A：はい、さくら内科クリニックでございます。
B：もしもし。今日の午後、診ていただきたいんですが、予約できますか。
A：はい。どのような症状でしょうか。
B：昨日の夜から熱があって、のどもかなり痛いんです。
A：さようでございますか。本日は三時半でしたら空いておりますが、いかがでしょうか。
B：じゃあ、三時半でお願いします。
A：かしこまりました。お名前をお願いいたします。
B：山田はるかと申します。保険証を持っていけばいいですか。
A：はい、保険証をお持ちください。それから、念のためマスクをしてお越しください。
passages.reference:
A: Sakura Internal Medicine Clinic, how can I help you?
B: Hello. I'd like to see a doctor this afternoon, if possible. Could I make an appointment?
A: Of course. What symptoms are you having?
B: I've had a fever since last night, and my throat is pretty sore too.
A: I'm sorry to hear that. We have an opening at 3:30 today. Would that work for you?
B: Yes, 3:30, please.
A: Certainly. May I have your name, please?
B: It's Haruka Yamada. Should I bring my insurance card?
A: Yes, please bring your insurance card. And just to be safe, please wear a mask when you come in.
passages.register: polite telephone English: professional receptionist, courteous patient
keyPoints: はい、…でございます = telephone greeting: 'Sakura Internal Medicine Clinic, how can I help you?'
診ていただきたいんですが = 'I'd like to see a doctor' (humble request, softened by が)
さようでございますか = sympathetic acknowledgment: 'I'm sorry to hear that'
三時半でしたら空いておりますが、いかがでしょうか = an offer: 'We have an opening at 3:30... would that work?'
保険証 = health insurance card; 念のため = just to be safe
passages.notes: Receptionist keigo (でございます, おります, お越しください) becomes professional courtesy in English. もしもし is a phone 'Hello', and the patient's name should be given in English order (Haruka Yamada).

passages.title: Curry again
passages.text:
A：ご飯できたよ。早く座って。
B：はーい。あ、またカレー？
A：文句があるなら食べなくていいよ。
C：まあまあ。お母さんのカレーはおいしいんだから。
B：別に文句じゃないって。昨日もカレーだったから言っただけ。
A：昨日のは残りだったの。今日のは新しく作ったんだから。
D：私、お代わりしてもいい？
C：ほら、お姉ちゃんはちゃんと味が分かってる。
passages.reference:
A: Dinner's ready. Come sit down.
B: Coming! Oh - curry again?
A: If you've got a problem with it, you don't have to eat it.
C: Now, now. Your mom's curry is delicious, you know.
B: I'm not complaining! I only said it 'cause we had curry yesterday too.
A: Yesterday's was leftovers. I made this one fresh today.
D: Can I have seconds?
C: See? Your sister knows good food when she tastes it.
passages.register: casual family English at the dinner table (warm teasing, contractions)
keyPoints: family-role address: father saying お母さん = 'your mom'; お姉ちゃん = 'your sister'
文句があるなら食べなくていい = 'If you've got a problem with it, you don't have to eat it' (mock-stern)
別に文句じゃないって = emphatic denial with って: 'I'm not complaining!'
昨日のは残り = yesterday's was leftovers
お代わり = seconds
passages.notes: Japanese families address each other by family role (the father calls his wife お母さん, the older daughter is お姉ちゃん); English uses 'your mom', 'your sister' or names. The speakers are mother (A), son (B), father (C), daughter (D); keep everyone casual.

passages.title: Materials for the manager
passages.text:
A：部長、今よろしいでしょうか。
B：ああ、いいよ。どうした？
A：来週の会議の資料ですが、先ほど完成いたしましたので、お目通しいただけますでしょうか。
B：早いね。じゃあ、あとで見ておくよ。
A：ありがとうございます。それと、取引先の田中様が、会議の日程を一日ずらしていただけないかとおっしゃっていたのですが…。
B：そうか。こっちは木曜日でも構わないって伝えておいてくれる？
A：承知いたしました。では、そのように申し伝えます。
B：よろしく。あ、会議室の予約も変更しておいてね。
A：かしこまりました。すぐに手配いたします。
passages.reference:
A: Excuse me, do you have a moment?
B: Sure. What's up?
A: I've just finished the materials for next week's meeting. Would you mind looking them over when you get a chance?
B: That was quick. I'll take a look later.
A: Thank you. Also, Mr. Tanaka from our client asked whether we might be able to push the meeting back a day...
B: I see. Could you let him know Thursday is fine on our end?
A: Certainly. I'll pass that along.
B: Thanks. Oh, and change the meeting room booking too, would you?
A: Will do. I'll take care of it right away.
passages.register: workplace English: deferential and formal from the subordinate, relaxed and friendly from the manager
keyPoints: 部長 as a form of address has no English equivalent; drop it or use 'Excuse me'
お目通しいただけますでしょうか = very deferential request: 'Would you mind looking them over?'
取引先の田中様 = Mr. Tanaka from our client
一日ずらしていただけないか = push (the meeting) back a day
申し伝えます = humble 'I'll pass that along'; keep the register asymmetry between A and B
passages.notes: The teaching point is asymmetry: A uses 謙譲語 and 尊敬語 (いたしました, おっしゃって, 申し伝えます) while the manager answers in plain casual forms. English shows this through softeners and formality on A's side and brevity on B's, not through titles.

passages.title: Garbage day
passages.text:
A：あ、こんにちは。いつもお世話になっております。
B：こんにちは。あの、ちょっとお話ししたいことがあるんですが、今お時間大丈夫ですか。
A：ええ、何でしょう。
B：実は、ゴミの日のことなんですけど、最近、燃えるゴミの日に缶が出されていることがあって…。
A：え、うちのかもしれません。すみません、先月引っ越してきたばかりで、まだ分別のルールがよく分かっていなくて。
B：ああ、そうでしたか。この辺り、ちょっと細かいんですよ。よかったら、町内会でもらった表、コピーしてお持ちしましょうか。
A：本当ですか。助かります。お手数をおかけしてすみません。
B：いえいえ、お互いさまですから。
passages.reference:
A: Oh, hello. Good to see you.
B: Hello. Um, there's something I wanted to mention, if you have a minute?
A: Sure, what is it?
B: Well, it's about garbage day. Lately there have sometimes been cans put out on burnable-garbage day...
A: Oh, that might be us. I'm sorry - we only moved in last month, and we're still not really clear on the sorting rules.
B: Oh, I see. The rules around here are a bit fussy. If you like, I could make you a copy of the chart we got from the neighborhood association.
A: Really? That would be a big help. Sorry to put you to the trouble.
B: Not at all. We all have to help each other out.
passages.register: polite, friendly English between neighbors, with softened indirect complaint
keyPoints: いつもお世話になっております = a set greeting; render as a friendly 'Good to see you', not 'thank you for always taking care of me'
〜ことがあって… = indirect, trailing complaint; keep it soft and unfinished
燃えるゴミ = burnable garbage; 分別 = sorting (recycling) rules
町内会 = neighborhood association
お互いさまですから = 'We all have to help each other out'
passages.notes: B raises a complaint without ever stating it directly, and A apologizes before being asked; the English should preserve that indirectness. うちの = 'ours / us' (the household), not 'my house'.

passages.title: Did you do the homework?
passages.text:
A: Hey, did you finish the homework for tomorrow?
B: Not yet. I totally forgot about it.
A: Seriously? It's due first thing in the morning.
B: I know, I know. Can I look at yours?
A: No way. But I can help you if you come over now.
B: Really? Thanks! I'll bring snacks.
passages.reference:
A：ねえ、明日の宿題、終わった？
B：まだ。すっかり忘れてた。
A：うそでしょ。朝一で出さなきゃいけないんだよ。
B：分かってる、分かってる。ちょっと見せてくれない？
A：だめ。でも、今からうちに来るなら手伝ってあげる。
B：本当？ありがとう！お菓子持っていくね。
passages.register: casual spoken Japanese between friends (普通体, dropped particles, contractions like 〜てた・〜なきゃ)
keyPoints: plain forms throughout: 終わった？, not 終わりましたか
totally forgot = すっかり忘れてた (contracted ている)
Seriously? = うそでしょ / まじで
due first thing in the morning = 朝一で出さなきゃいけない
come over = うちに来る; I'll bring = 持っていく (direction toward the friend's place)
passages.notes: Using です/ます here would sound distant between friends. 'Come over' is うちに来る, and 'I'll bring' must be 持っていく from B's point of view, not 持ってくる.

passages.title: A table by the window
passages.text:
A: Good evening. Do you have a reservation?
B: Yes, under the name Kimura. Two people at seven.
A: Kimura, party of two... Yes, here you are. We have a table by the window for you. Right this way, please.
B: Thank you. Oh, is there somewhere we can leave our coats?
A: Of course. I'll take them for you. Here is your ticket.
B: Great. And could we see the drink menu first?
A: Certainly. I'll bring it right away.
passages.reference:
A：いらっしゃいませ。ご予約のお客様でいらっしゃいますか。
B：はい、木村で予約しています。七時に二人です。
A：木村様、二名様ですね…。はい、承っております。窓側のお席をご用意しております。どうぞこちらへ。
B：ありがとうございます。あ、コートはどこかに預けられますか。
A：もちろんでございます。こちらでお預かりいたします。こちらが番号札でございます。
B：どうも。それから、先に飲み物のメニューを見せてもらえますか。
A：かしこまりました。すぐにお持ちいたします。
passages.register: restaurant service Japanese: staff use keigo (様, 承る, お預かりいたします); the customer uses plain です/ます
keyPoints: Good evening (restaurant greeting) = いらっしゃいませ
under the name Kimura = 木村で予約しています; staff say 木村様
party of two = 二名様
I'll take them for you = お預かりいたします; ticket = 番号札
Certainly = かしこまりました; I'll bring it = お持ちいたします
passages.notes: The customer never uses 様 or humble forms about himself; the staff always do. 'Good evening' at a restaurant door is いらっしゃいませ, not こんばんは.

passages.title: Leaving a message for a client
passages.text:
A: Hello, this is Sato from Aoba Design. May I speak to Ms. Ogawa, please?
B: I'm afraid she's in a meeting right now. Would you like to leave a message?
A: Yes, please. Could you tell her that I've sent the revised estimate by email?
B: Certainly. Is there anything else?
A: If possible, I'd appreciate it if she could call me back by tomorrow afternoon.
B: Understood. I'll make sure she gets the message.
A: Thank you very much. Goodbye.
passages.reference:
A：お世話になっております。青葉デザインの佐藤と申します。小川様はいらっしゃいますでしょうか。
B：申し訳ございません。小川はただいま会議中でございます。よろしければ、ご伝言を承りましょうか。
A：はい、お願いいたします。修正したお見積もりをメールでお送りしたとお伝えいただけますか。
B：かしこまりました。ほかに何かございますか。
A：できましたら、明日の午後までにお電話をいただけると助かります。
B：承知いたしました。確かに申し伝えます。
A：よろしくお願いいたします。失礼いたします。
passages.register: business telephone Japanese: full keigo (尊敬語 for the other company, 謙譲語 for oneself and one's own colleagues)
keyPoints: opener: お世話になっております + 〜と申します, not こんにちは
uchi/soto: A says 小川様 but B, her colleague, says plain 小川 with no 様
May I speak to = いらっしゃいますでしょうか; leave a message = ご伝言を承りましょうか
I've sent ... = お送りした (謙譲語); tell her = お伝えいただけますか
Goodbye on a business call = 失礼いたします
passages.notes: The key trap is in-group reference: when speaking to an outsider, B refers to her own colleague without 様 or honorifics (小川はただいま会議中でございます). 'I'll make sure she gets the message' becomes 確かに申し伝えます.

passages.title: Office hours
passages.text:
A: Excuse me, Professor Mori. Do you have a few minutes?
B: Sure, come in. What can I do for you?
A: I wanted to ask you about my term paper. I'm worried my topic is still too broad.
B: Let me see your outline... Hmm, yes, it's a bit broad. Why don't you focus on just one region?
A: I see. Then I'll rewrite it and bring it to you next week, if that's all right.
B: That's fine. Come by on Tuesday afternoon.
A: Thank you so much for your time.
passages.reference:
A：失礼します。森先生、今少しお時間よろしいでしょうか。
B：ああ、どうぞ入って。どうしたの？
A：期末レポートのことでご相談したいんですが、テーマがまだ広すぎるんじゃないかと思いまして。
B：構成を見せてくれる？……うん、確かにちょっと広いね。一つの地域に絞ってみたらどうかな。
A：なるほど。では書き直して、よろしければ来週またお持ちします。
B：いいよ。火曜日の午後においで。
A：お忙しいところ、ありがとうございました。
passages.register: student-to-professor Japanese: the student uses です/ます with keigo (お時間よろしいでしょうか, ご相談, お持ちします); the professor answers in plain, friendly forms
keyPoints: Professor Mori = 森先生 (never 森教授さん)
Do you have a few minutes? = 今少しお時間よろしいでしょうか
ask you about = ご相談したい (謙譲語); bring it to you = お持ちします
Why don't you focus on = 〜に絞ってみたらどうかな (professor's casual suggestion)
Thank you for your time = お忙しいところ、ありがとうございました
passages.notes: The register is asymmetric: the student must not answer in plain forms, and the professor would sound odd using keigo to a student. 失礼します on entering the office has no English counterpart but is expected in Japanese.
